blocks.body: Does $x^5 - 3x + 1 = 0$ have a solution between $0$ and $1$? At $x = 0$ the left side is $1$, at $x = 1$ it is $-1$. If the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen, it must cross the $x$-axis in between. That pen picture is the intuition behind continuity, and the conclusion is the intermediate value theorem. Its proof needs a special property of the real numbers.

blocks.title: Continuity
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be defined on an interval $I$ and let $a \in I$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that
$$x \in I,\ |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(a)| < \varepsilon.$$
When $a$ is an interior point of $I$, this says exactly that $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$ (see [[limits]]); at an endpoint of $I$ it is the same condition with $x$ approaching from inside $I$ only. $f$ is continuous on $I$ if it is continuous at every point of $I$.

In words: small changes in the input produce small changes in the output.

blocks.title: Three ways to fail
blocks.body:
Continuity at an interior point $a$ makes three demands: $f(a)$ is defined, the limit at $a$ exists, and the two agree. Each can fail.

1. A hole. Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ for $x \ne 1$ and $f(1) = 0$. The limit at $1$ is $2$ but the value is $0$; setting $f(1) = 2$ repairs this (a removable discontinuity).
2. A jump. The floor function $\lfloor x \rfloor$, the greatest integer not exceeding $x$, is $0$ just left of $1$ and $1$ on $[1, 2)$: the one-sided limits at $1$ differ. The same happens at every integer.
3. Oscillation. Let $f(x) = \sin(1/x)$ for $x \ne 0$ and $f(0) = 0$. There is no limit at $0$ at all.

Note that $1/x$ is continuous at every point of its domain; $0$ is not in the domain. The pen picture is only a guide: $x\sin(1/x)$, with value $0$ at $0$, wiggles infinitely often near $0$ yet is continuous there, as $|x\sin(1/x)| \le |x|$.

blocks.title: Building continuous functions
blocks.body:
By the limit laws ([[limits]]), if $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $a$, so are $f + g$, $f - g$, $fg$, and $f/g$ if $g(a) \ne 0$. Hence polynomials are continuous everywhere, and rational functions wherever the denominator is nonzero.

If $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ at $g(a)$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at $a$: for a tolerance $\varepsilon$ on $f$, continuity of $f$ gives a tolerance $\eta$ to demand of $g$, and continuity of $g$ gives the $\delta$.

We accept without proof that $\sqrt x$, $a^x$, $\log_a x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous on their domains. For $\sin$ it is quick: the identity $\sin x - \sin a = 2\cos\frac{x + a}{2}\sin\frac{x - a}{2}$ (from the addition formulas in [[trig]]) and $|\sin t| \le |t|$ give $|\sin x - \sin a| \le |x - a|$. (Here $|\sin t| \le |t|$ holds because $\sin t < t$ for $0 < t < \pi/2$, shown in [[limits]], while $|\sin t| \le 1 < |t|$ when $|t| \ge \pi/2$.)

blocks.title: Bisection, and why the real numbers matter
blocks.body:
To hunt for the root of $f(x) = x^5 - 3x + 1$ in $[0, 1]$, where $f(0) > 0 > f(1)$, evaluate $f$ at the midpoint and keep the half where the sign changes:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{interval} & \text{midpoint } m & f(m) \\ \hline [0, 1] & 0.5 & -0.469 \\ [0, 0.5] & 0.25 & 0.251 \\ [0.25, 0.5] & 0.375 & -0.118 \\ [0.25, 0.375] & 0.3125 & 0.065 \end{array}$$
Each step halves the interval, so after $20$ steps the root is trapped in an interval of length $2^{-20} < 10^{-6}$; it is $0.33473\ldots$.

But why must there be a root at all? That shrinking nested intervals of real numbers always close in on a real number is a form of the completeness of $\mathbb R$, and it is genuinely needed: over the rationals, $x^2 - 2$ is negative at $1$ and positive at $2$, but no rational number has square $2$.

The proof below uses the least upper bound property: every nonempty set $S$ of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound $\sup S$, a number $s$ with $x \le s$ for all $x \in S$ such that no smaller number has this property. This is a basic axiom of the real numbers, taken as given here (see [[real-numbers]]).

blocks.title: Intermediate value theorem
blocks.body: Let $f$ be continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$, and let $y$ be a number strictly between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. Then there is a $c$ with $a < c < b$ and $f(c) = y$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We treat the case $f(a) < y < f(b)$; the case $f(a) > y > f(b)$ follows by applying it to $-f$ and $-y$.

First, sign persistence: if $c \in [a, b]$ and $f(c) < y$, then $f(x) < y$ for all $x \in [a, b]$ near $c$; take $\varepsilon = y - f(c)$ in the definition of continuity. Likewise if $f(c) > y$.

Let $S = \{x \in [a, b] : f(x) < y\}$. It contains $a$ and is bounded above by $b$, so it has a least upper bound $c = \sup S$, with $a \le c \le b$. We rule out $f(c) < y$ and $f(c) > y$.

Suppose $f(c) < y$. Then $c \ne b$, as $f(b) > y$, and by sign persistence there is $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < y$ for all $x \in [a, b]$ with $|x - c| < \delta$. Any $x$ with $c < x < \min(c + \delta, b)$ is then in $S$, contradicting that $c$ is an upper bound of $S$.

Suppose $f(c) > y$. Then $c \ne a$, as $f(a) < y$, and by sign persistence there is $\delta$ with $0 < \delta \le c - a$ such that $f(x) > y$ on $(c - \delta, c]$. So no point of $(c - \delta, c]$ is in $S$, nor any point above $c$. Hence $c - \delta$ is an upper bound of $S$ smaller than $c$: a contradiction.

Therefore $f(c) = y$, and $c \ne a, b$ since $f(a) \ne y \ne f(b)$.

blocks.title: Largest and smallest values
blocks.body: A second theorem of the same kind, also resting on completeness, is the extreme value theorem: a function continuous on a closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ is bounded there and attains a largest and a smallest value. We state it without proof (the proof is best seen through [[compactness]]). Both hypotheses matter: on the open interval $(0, 1)$, $1/x$ is unbounded and $x$ has no largest value; on $[-1, 1]$, the function equal to $1/x$ for $x \ne 0$ and $0$ at $0$ is unbounded, because it is not continuous at $0$.

blocks.title: Counting real roots
blocks.body: Show that $x^5 - 3x + 1 = 0$ has at least three real solutions.
blocks.solution:
$f(x) = x^5 - 3x + 1$ is a polynomial, hence continuous, and
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline f(x) & -25 & 3 & 1 & -1 & 27 \end{array}$$
The sign changes on $[-2, -1]$, $[0, 1]$ and $[1, 2]$, so the intermediate value theorem with $y = 0$ gives a root in each of $(-2, -1)$, $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 2)$. These intervals do not overlap, so the three roots are different.

With derivatives one can show there are exactly three ([[deriv-applications]]).

blocks.title: Gluing two pieces
blocks.body: For which value of $k$ is the function $f(x) = kx + 1$ for $x \le 2$, $f(x) = x^2$ for $x > 2$, continuous everywhere?
blocks.solution: Away from $x = 2$, $f$ agrees near each point with a polynomial, so it is continuous there. At $x = 2$ the value and the limit from the left are $2k + 1$, while the limit from the right is $\lim_{x\to 2^+} x^2 = 4$. They must agree: $2k + 1 = 4$, so $k = \tfrac32$.

blocks.title: A fixed point
blocks.body: Let $f\colon [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ be continuous. Prove that $f(c) = c$ for some $c \in [0, 1]$.
blocks.solution: Let $g(x) = f(x) - x$, continuous on $[0, 1]$. As $f$ takes values in $[0, 1]$, $g(0) = f(0) \ge 0$ and $g(1) = f(1) - 1 \le 0$. If either is $0$, take $c = 0$ or $c = 1$. Otherwise $g(0) > 0 > g(1)$, and the intermediate value theorem gives $c \in (0, 1)$ with $g(c) = 0$, that is, $f(c) = c$. In pictures: the graph of $f$ crosses the unit square from left to right, so it meets the diagonal $y = x$.

blocks.title: Half the distance in half the time
blocks.body: A runner covers $10$ km in exactly $60$ minutes, at a varying pace. Prove that there is a $30$-minute period during which she covers exactly $5$ km.
blocks.solution:
Let $d(t)$ be the distance covered after $t$ minutes, continuous with $d(0) = 0$ and $d(60) = 10$. For $0 \le t \le 30$ the distance covered in the $30$ minutes from time $t$ is $g(t) = d(t + 30) - d(t)$, a continuous function with
$$g(0) + g(30) = \big(d(30) - d(0)\big) + \big(d(60) - d(30)\big) = 10.$$
So either $g(0) = g(30) = 5$, or one is above $5$ and the other below, and the intermediate value theorem gives $t \in (0, 30)$ with $g(t) = 5$.

For $n$ pieces, let $g(t) = d(t + \tfrac{60}{n}) - d(t)$: the $n$ values $g(0), g(\tfrac{60}{n}), \ldots, g(\tfrac{60(n - 1)}{n})$ add up to $10$, so they are neither all above nor all below $\tfrac{10}{n}$, and the same argument gives a $\tfrac{60}{n}$-minute period covering exactly $\tfrac{10}{n}$ km.

This is the universal chord theorem of Paul Lévy: if $f$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$ and $f(0) = f(1)$, then for every positive integer $n$ there is an $x \in [0, 1 - \tfrac1n]$ with $f(x + \tfrac1n) = f(x)$, a horizontal chord of length $\tfrac1n$. (Apply it to $f(s) = d(60s) - 10s$.) For a length that is not of the form $\tfrac1n$, such a chord need not exist. For example, the increasing pace plan
$$d(t) = \frac{19t}{120} + \frac12\sin^2\frac{\pi t}{24}$$
has $d(0) = 0$ and $d(60) = 9.5 + \tfrac12\sin^2\tfrac{5\pi}{2} = 10$, but since $\sin^2(\theta + \pi) = \sin^2\theta$, every $24$-minute period covers $d(t + 24) - d(t) = \tfrac{19 \cdot 24}{120} = 3.8$ km, never $4$ km.

blocks.body:
- The theorem needs continuity on the whole closed interval: $1/x$ is negative at $-1$ and positive at $1$ but never $0$, and it is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$.
- The converse is false: $\sin(1/x)$, with value $0$ at $0$, takes every value in $[-1, 1]$ on every interval $[0, b]$ with $b > 0$, yet it is discontinuous at $0$.

The [[mvt]] combines continuity with derivatives, and continuous functions on $[a, b]$ can be integrated ([[riemann-integral]]). The extreme value theorem is really about [[compactness]], and the intermediate value theorem about connectedness. A limit of continuous functions need not be continuous unless the convergence is uniform ([[uniform-convergence]]). The fixed point example is the one-dimensional case of Brouwer's fixed point theorem: every continuous map from a closed disc (or ball) to itself has a fixed point.

1. Show that $\cos x = x$ has a solution in $[0, \pi/2]$.
2. Show that every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real root.
3. A continuous function $f\colon [0, 2] \to \mathbb R$ satisfies $f(0) = f(2)$. Show that $f(c) = f(c + 1)$ for some $c \in [0, 1]$.
4. Where is $f(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ continuous? Sketch its graph.
